stories.Headline: Trump admin to receive $100 million in compute credits for AI science initiative
stories.Summary:
National Compute, a new company that has pooled computing power from major tech companies, plans to donate $100 million worth of computing credits to the Trump administration, according to two people familiar with the matter. The credits are expected to be announced on Thursday at an event with White House Office of Science and Technology Policy Director Michael Kratsios. They will support the administration's Genesis mission, a government-wide push to use AI to accelerate scientific discovery. The donation would give Genesis Mission researchers access to advanced computing resources at a time when smaller labs and companies can struggle to secure capacity for frontier research, because major providers often prioritise long-term contracts with the largest AI labs.

National Compute is building what it calls the National Compute Grid, a network intended to pool computing capacity from multiple providers and make it available to researchers, companies and government agencies. A draft paper reviewed by POLITICO compares the grid to the power grid or interstate highway system and describes it as a shared network connecting resources that are currently isolated. The grid is intended to bring together capacity from sources including labs and cloud providers that deploy Nvidia and AMD processors and Google's tensor processing units. Users could buy compute as needed, reserve capacity for larger projects or connect their own systems, and would only pay for the power they use. National Compute is backed by chipmakers, cloud and infrastructure providers including Vultr and Crusoe, and universities, and is financed by venture capitalists and institutional investors including universities and pension funds. It aims to pool 2 gigawatts of computing capacity by 2030, with 750 megawatts allocated to date.

National Compute Cofounder Anjney Midha said he thinks there should be thousands more companies like Anthropic and OpenAI, and that reducing the barrier to entry and increasing compute access would let researchers and scientists do what they do best. National Compute is also launching a Grid Defense program that lets government agencies test AI models through Marshall, an agent embedded in the grid, before deciding whether the models are safe enough to deploy. Agencies can set their own testing procedures, according to Midha, and those details are designed to remain confidential in part to keep frontier models from learning how to evade the evaluations. The agent would coordinate testing and return anonymized results to researchers, and the government would be able to see the results while labs decide voluntarily whether to release a model. Midha described the approach as continuous frontier alignment monitoring at scale, and National Compute said the effort was created in response to high-profile incidents involving AI agents, including attacks on companies reported by AI labs over the summer. The Grid Defense program entered invite-only early access in June with some government agencies.

The initiative comes as the Trump administration looks for ways to expand access to computing power as part of a largely light-touch approach to AI regulation that has prioritized winning a race with China to build the most advanced models. The administration has described its research push as a "golden age of science," which will be celebrated at the Thursday event. The White House declined to comment on the donation and the computing network. The articles also note that the AI Infrastructure Coalition was established in the US on November 19, 2025, with members including Google, Microsoft and Andreessen Horowitz, and focuses on policy advocacy rather than operating a grid. The National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource has supported over 600 research projects and 6,000 students as of 2026 updates and has been transitioning from a pilot to operational status. India's National AI Compute Grid is set to roll out in phases through 2026, China reported 1,882 EFLOPS of intelligent computing capacity by March 2026, and the AI Energy Management Alliance launched on September 16, 2026, estimating a potential $733 million in avoided power system costs per GW.
